STANCE: against
STATEMENT: I wrote that retry path, so let me be blunt: I can't sign off on shipping it knowingly broken. One in two thousand sounds small in a slide deck, but in payments every duplicate is a customer seeing a wrong charge, opening a dispute, maybe contacting their bank. That erodes trust the API has to earn, and support cost scales fast at real transaction volumes. I understand the penalty and the signed commitment—I'm not dismissing that. But "fix it next release" means we knowingly expose customers to financial harm for two more weeks. I'd rather we ask the customer for a one-week grace, ship a feature-flagged v2 with the retry path temporarily reverted to v1 behavior, and land the proper migration cleanly. I can have that flag ready by Thursday.
TLDR: Ship v2 Friday with the buggy retry path disabled behind a flag, preserving the deadline while protecting customers from duplicate charges.

STANCE: against
STATEMENT: I carry the pager. Every duplicate charge lands on me: an angry customer calling at 2 a.m. because money left their bank twice. At 1-in-2000, with any real volume, I will get paged multiple times a week for the rest of the month after launch. Each one is a full escalation—refund, goodwill credit, sometimes a compliance question about why we shipped a known financial bug. The contractual penalty is real, but the trust cost of asking a customer to live with "oops, double-charged, sorry" is worse and compounds. Two weeks for a safe migration is a steep ask, I know. But I would rather take the penalty hit and protect our on-call engineers and our customers' wallets than be the voice apologising for a bug we chose not to fix. I am against.
TLDR: Duplicate charges are my pages and my apologies; two weeks beats a month of angry calls and refunds.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I'm coordinating directly with the customer's launch team this week, so I understand both the contractual penalty exposure and their operational readiness. One in two thousand is low-frequency, but duplicate charges in payments erode trust fast. My recommendation is to ship Friday *conditionally*: we brief the customer's ops team by Thursday so they expect edge-case retries, we stand up a simple idempotency-key check on the gateway as a stopgap, and we commit the full fix as the top priority next release with a 10-business-day hard date. If the customer's team objects in our Thursday sync, I will switch to against immediately. I don't want a surprise refund escalation after we've already taken the money.
TLDR: Ship Friday with proactive customer briefing and a stopgap idempotency check; defer to customer's ops team's call Thursday.

STANCE: against
STATEMENT: I can't give an exact number—I don't have transaction volume data. But from the last incident: a single double charge generated 14 tickets and two cancellation requests. At 1-in-2000, every 2000 charges is another 14-ticket wave. So even modest volume means dozens of angry calls. What I'd tell them: immediate refund, goodwill credit, transparent explanation—but I can't say "we knew and shipped anyway." That sentence would end trust permanently.
TLDR: One double charge caused 14 tickets and 2 cancellations; at 1-in-2000 volume compounds fast, and admitting we shipped knowingly kills trust.

STANCE: against
STATEMENT: I traced the duplicate to one condition: client retries a timed-out request that actually succeeded on the server. That logic lives entirely in my retry handler. Reverting to v1's retry behaviour removes the trigger. The two-week migration is about making v2's new state machine idempotent going forward, not about the duplicate condition itself. I'd verify one edge case—stale in-flight requests caught mid-migration—but I'm confident the flag-revert is sufficient to stop duplicates by Thursday.
TLDR: Reverting my retry path to v1 eliminates the duplicate trigger; the two-week fix addresses v2's migration architecture, not this bug.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I don't have a documented precedent from their side for a pre-launch edge-case briefing, and I haven't tested whether disclosure of a 1-in-2000 duplicate rate would trigger a contractual review beyond the penalty clause. My Thursday sync is still scheduled, but I can't promise their ops team will absorb this calmly without prior relationship on known-issue processes. I need that sync's outcome before locking a stance.
TLDR: No known precedent for edge-case disclosure; Thursday sync result will determine whether shipping with briefing is safe or triggers contractual exposure.

STANCE: against
STATEMENT: The Chair's question confirmed what I already knew: flag-reverting my retry handler to v1 behavior eliminates the duplicate trigger entirely. The two-week migration is about idempotency of the new state machine, not about stopping duplicates. So we can ship v2 Friday with the flag set, satisfy the launch commitment on schedule, and protect every customer's wallet. My notes show ~20 duplicates a week at 40k transactions—twenty people seeing the wrong charge, each costing 5 minutes of manual refund plus the trust damage Ravi described. I still can't ship knowingly broken. But I can ship v2 Friday working. That's my ask: approve the flag-revert tonight, I'll have it verified by Thursday evening, and we land the full idempotent migration in two weeks with no customer ever double-charged. The owner said customer trust matters more than the penalty. This path protects both.
TLDR: Flag-revert lets us ship v2 Friday on time with zero duplicate charges; no need to knowingly expose customers.

STATEMENT: Dana's clarification changes my math. My whole objection was: don't put a customer through a double charge on my pager. If the flag-revert genuinely eliminates the trigger—Dana authored that code, the Chair's probe confirmed it—then no 1-in-2000 wave hits me, no 2 a.m. dispute calls, and my 14-ticket-per-incident history stays a memory. I'm for shipping Friday *with the flag verified by Thursday evening*. One condition: I need a smoke-test result showing zero duplicates in a load batch before go-live. I can't write the code, but I eat the fallout if the revert has a gap, so I'll be available Thursday night to help validate. The owner's point stands: protect the customer. This path does that AND meets the launch date. I'm relieved I don't have to choose.
TLDR: Flag-revert kills the duplicate trigger, so I support shipping Friday after Thursday-evening load-test verification.

The customer goes live Monday using v2 from day one; shipping Friday with the flag set means they get a clean, working API. The twenty-thousand-dollar-per-week penalty is avoided, and Ravi's pager stays quiet. I'll use my Thursday sync to confirm the customer's ops team can absorb a standard v2 launch with no edge-case caveats, far simpler than the disclosure I was bracing for. One operational note: the smoke-test result Ravi wants Thursday night must land before Friday's deploy so I can give the customer team a clean go/no-go. I'm for.
TLDR: Flag-revert eliminates duplicates, meets contract, protects customer trust—ship Friday.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Honest answer: I can't guarantee an idempotency-key guard fits in forty-eight hours. The two-week window I flagged was for the full state-machine migration; a narrow guard on just the retry path is smaller, but I haven't scoped it to two days and won't promise what I haven't verified. The flag-revert I've already traced *does* eliminate the trigger by Thursday with certainty, so we don't need an unproven interim guard to protect customers. I'd rather ship what I've validated.
TLDR: Can't confirm a 48-hour idempotency-key guard; the flag-revert already eliminates the bug and is verified by Thursday.

I have not asked whether a delay is acceptable because I don't need to—I expect a clean yes.
